question.text: As per SEBI regulations, when was entry load abolished for mutual fund schemes in India, and what was the rationale?

answer.text: August 2009 — to prevent the practice of using investor money to pay distributor commissions upfront, making costs more transparent
April 2012 — to align Indian mutual fund regulations with international standards
January 2013 — to coincide with the launch of direct plans for mutual funds
March 2006 — as part of the first comprehensive mutual fund regulation reform

explanation.text: The Logic: SEBI banned entry load on mutual fund schemes with effect from August 2009. The rationale, as widely understood in the industry, was that entry load was being used to pay upfront distributor commissions out of investor money at the point of sale, creating a non-transparent cost layer for the investor. Abolishing entry load aligned the investor's purchase price with the NAV (subject to applicable transaction charges/stamp duty as introduced later), and shifted distributor compensation toward trail commissions paid by the AMC out of the TER. The Trap: April 2012 and January 2013 are associated with subsequent mutual-fund regulatory actions (such as the introduction of direct plans in January 2013), not the entry-load ban. March 2006 predates the entry-load abolition entirely. The reform was specifically targeted at entry load, not a broad-based first-time mutual-fund regulation. Note: The cited NISM Series V-A workbook pages confirm that entry loads are banned and that current distributor compensation is trail-based, but they do not state the specific August 2009 effective date or the rationale in the form used above. The August 2009 date and the transparency-and-commission rationale are referenced here from the underlying SEBI circular as general regulatory history, not as a workbook-page citation.
